segment:
She was blushing like an idiot, she knew; what business was it of hers, anyway? It came to her in that moment how strange this would all have seemed even two days earlier. If you had told her then she was going to be here now, she wouldn’t have believed it. She said as much to him. He nodded, with that thoughtful smile.
“I know.”
He didn’t seem to think it necessary to explain further. But the air was becoming suddenly, unpleasantly warm inside the car, and she opened her window without thinking. The late-summer evening was warm, though not humid, and there was something of sea tang in the wind.
She got out of the car before it came to a full stop, leaving him to carry her bags and find a parking place. He smiled as he saw her go, she thought. It had nothing to do with her looks. It wasn’t her good looks that had got her this job; it wasn’t those that made his eyes stay on her face.
She walked slowly, not wanting to rush at it—but not wanting to stand and stare, either. The glass walls were completely reflective, and showed a small, narrow woman in black jeans and an open-necked yellow shirt, her dark hair shining in the light of the setting sun, which was now just peeping over the ridge on the far side. She couldn’t see inside.
There was no one else about. She paused to light a cigarette, then looked around again, taking stock. There was something unusual about this place. The low glass building stood in stark contrast to the forest it rose from. There was no sign of life; it could have been a deserted office building on some strange planet.
The buildings were clustered together, all of them seeming to be made of concrete and glass. There were four other buildings behind the one she was in, each one set back a few feet from its neighbors. She was looking down at the parking lot, with one long row of cars parked nose to tail, facing away from her. A paved road ran parallel to the parking lot and curved around to the left, heading up toward the ridge. There was a large redwood grove to the right of the building; the sun shone through the trees, casting shadows on the grass and making the trees seem like giants standing guard over the parking lot.
text:

“We’re the last ones here,” Mara said aloud, to break her silence.
Her driver was a white man in his late forties, bald, with a lined and thoughtful face. He gave her a friendly smile, which she returned.
“Not much traffic on Route One after rush hour. We got lucky.”
“How long have you been coming out to this place, Mr. …?” She couldn’t remember his name, from her phone call; she was still reeling from the drive in and the view of the buildings, rising in a terrace toward the ridge above them.
“Call me Hal,” he said. “I don’t mind. I’ve been coming here for two years, on and off.”

segment:
she asked, hesitantly.
He shrugged and took a small key from his pocket.
“It’s pretty enough, that’s for sure. As to the people who work there, I’m not much qualified to say. I do the driving, so I don’t get into any of the meetings. I do hear talk, though, as you can imagine. Most of the staff I pick up are pretty happy, though it seems to me like the older ones don’t get along too well with the younger ones. But then, they wouldn’t. The same thing goes on in my brother-in-law’s place of business, and there’s nothing wrong with his company at all. Just people are people.”
“Yes, I suppose so,” she said. She was trying to look as neutral and bland as she could. The man wasn’t likely to be used to interviewing people about their work or their colleagues, and she didn’t want him to feel uncomfortable; that wouldn’t help her in getting into Fulcrum, after all.
“You think you’ll get the job?” he asked, a hint of friendliness in his voice.
“Well, I don’t know,” she said. “I thought I knew my stuff, but then we got to the nonverbal questions, and I felt like I was failing that part pretty badly.”
He gave her an easy smile. “Well, you might do better than you think you have. My wife and me, we watched those shows where people tell on each other all the time. Lying is just another form of dishonesty,” he said, with a small shrug. “But I guess that’s the point, isn’t it? Anyway, you should get along fine with them there. They’re usually pretty good people.”
They pulled up to the door and she let herself out, and Hal wished her luck again with a wave as he drove away.
She stood alone for a minute, watching the light die off the building in the distance, before she turned to look at the door again. A small card was inserted into the top of the slot, which read, “Fulcrum Research Center.” The words were printed in bold letters, and there was a number underneath.
She wasn’t sure what to do next. Should she call them, or just wait? There was nothing in her instructions about any of this, but then again, there was no one to ask. So she waited for someone to come along who knew something about this place.
She didn’t have long to wait. A young man stepped out from the building, his white shirt wrinkled at the sides. He looked her up and down quickly and smiled.
“Hi,” he said. “You must be Mara.”

segment:
she asked. He glanced at her; her hair was loose, tumbling over her shoulders, still a little damp from the shower she’d taken before setting out; she felt self-conscious, but had no hairpins; they’d gone down the drain. Her face was pale after the drive; she hoped it didn’t show.
He shrugged. “I come when I can. It’s an interesting group.”
“I know,” she said with a smile. “That’s what I mean—it’s not like a regular job for you, is it?”
“I’ve got a job.” He was opening the trunk of his car with a remote device; she caught him looking at her with interest and thought, he means the interview.
“What do you do?” She pulled her suitcase from the trunk.
“I work for the F.B.I.,” he said, simply. “In the Behavioral Analysis Unit.”
She was a psychologist, herself, and had known about the Unit. It was an elite group of investigators, known colloquially as mind-hunters. They specialized in analyzing the behavior of violent criminals, using psychological profiling to identify characteristics common to offenders of a particular type. Most of them were former or current cops. She couldn’t imagine why one would come to Fulcrum.
“Do you … bring work here with you?” she asked, thinking, I can’t picture that.
“Sometimes,” he said, smiling. “I’ve been on the job a long time. They don’t call me very often, these days.”
He must be pretty good at what he did to have made it that far up in the organization. He’d certainly not been lying about having done the work for long.
“Did you bring any files?” she asked.
He shrugged. “No files,” he said. “But I brought the case.”
They stepped out from the shade of the car, and Mara heard the sharp intake of breath behind her as Hal caught sight of the buildings. The sun was falling, slanting gold and red across the grass on the terrace and through the tall glass walls. The white structure at the top gleamed, and she saw, not the light, but the reflection of the water that had fallen down its length and pooled in the shallow pool at the bottom of its vertical drop.
“That’s beautiful,” Hal said quietly. He gestured at the trees to one side of the lawn. “But it’s the trees that got me.”
“What about them?” She was already halfway across the lawn, looking at the trees on the other side. The sun had already gone behind them, but the light played upon their leaves, turning them to gold and a deep purple.
“The way they change color,” he said simply. “It’s magical.”

segment:
She asked this by way of keeping him talking until she could compose herself.
The driver gave her a surprised smile, but replied civilly. “Don’t call me ‘sir,’ Miss…” He paused.
“Call me Mara,” she suggested, trying not to sound flustered. “Or Maranata, if you like—it’s my whole first name.”
“Mara,” he said. “Yes, I do think much of it, though. Why? Have you come for the program?”
“I have.” She nodded, relieved that he didn’t seem to find the idea strange. “And you? What about you?”
“I’m on the Board.” He looked at her curiously as he drove along a twisting access road through the trees, toward what appeared to be a paved parking space in front of the entrance.
“So am I,” she said. “I mean … will be.”
“Oh.” She saw him glance in the rearview mirror. “So you’ve seen the buildings before. But not in this light.”
“No.” He pulled to a stop in front of the building, and let the engine run for a minute to allow Mara to adjust herself. “It’s very beautiful,” she said.
He nodded. “Quite an amazing place.”
She opened her eyes wider to take in the view of the redwood forest stretching back from the terrace toward the ridge above, and breathed a deep sigh.
“So do you mean I will be your colleague?” she asked him, putting a smile on her face as she spoke. She didn’t know whether it was appropriate or not, and hoped he wouldn’t find it strange; his was the first face she had seen upon arrival in California, and she would rather like it to be a friendly one.
“I … think so,” he said, a little hesitantly. “I suppose it will depend on how things go for you—in terms of whether you complete the program or not.”
She laughed, wondering what would happen to her if she failed to complete the program; what sort of fate awaited those who washed out. But he seemed too much at ease with the idea of being washed out to be alarmed by it.
He turned off the car engine and got out of his seat to help her with her luggage; he smiled warmly when he saw how little she had brought with her—two suitcases, neither more than a few feet long.
“Not many clothes?” he asked as they stood at the door of the entrance, waiting for a staff member to unlock it so that Mara could enter. She shook her head in response.

segment:
He glanced at her, then away. He’d caught the slight hesitation in her voice—she’d nearly called him “Mr. Hal,” before correcting herself—and she didn’t know if he was offended, amused, or just disinterested.
“Well,” he said after a moment, “I don’t think there’s anything better. There’s other schools, for cue reading and calibrating, of course. But I’ve been to the top ones, and this is the best.”
He paused, as though she was going to say something, but she just nodded.
“And so—” Hal finished his thought with a shrug. “I keep coming back here, when I can. They’ve got some … special programs for people who work in politics. It’s … been interesting, to say the least.” He cleared his throat.
Mara felt that this was an opening of some sort; an invitation to ask more, or even volunteer information. The question hung between them like a spider’s thread, the faintest line against the open sky. Should she follow it? She had a feeling that there was some risk involved.
She wondered why that should be, and wondered why she felt her heart beating faster at the thought. She hadn’t been taking any drugs; that was certain. The two pills of Valium that she had taken the night before were long gone from her system. It had been easy enough to smuggle them; she had brought only her passport and driver’s license with her, but Hal had asked for her credit card, and the pills had been easy to slip in. She had carried a few more in her purse, just in case, but it seemed that there hadn’t been any need.
The Valium had allowed her to sleep last night, but it hadn’t helped at all with the pain. The headache was still with her today, worse than before; she had taken two ibuprofen pills and an aspirin, but they hadn’t made much difference. The pain throbbed in time with her heartbeat, in a rhythm so slow and measured that she felt as though her head must be swollen with water.
The thought of taking another drug now, a narcotic, was unappealing, even dangerous. She wasn’t sure how her body would react; it had been six months since the accident, and the painkillers prescribed after that hadn’t helped much. She was still taking them, but not regularly; only when the pain was very bad, which was most days.

she blundered out, wondering whether she should have come after all. She couldn’t back out now; he had her luggage in the car.
Hal smiled at her again.
“That depends on what you mean.”
“I mean—is it what people say? What they told me, on the phone?”
He turned onto the driveway that led to the reception area, and she looked out the window again. The view of the bay, visible in glimpses through the trees, had taken her breath away.
“Is it strange?” she asked. “What are you, all of you? Are you—is this a cult?”
Hal’s smile didn’t leave his face. He brought the car to a stop just in front of the door, and let his foot rest on the brake, the car idling quietly.
“This is Fulcrum,” he said simply. “Fulcrum is what it is.”
And then she saw something that froze her throat. A young fellow, no more than seventeen or so, walked out from one of the buildings set farther back on the hillside—she could see nothing in detail, but she recognized him, all right—the lean lanky body, the dark hair, and the long white sleeves of his shirt.
“Jesus,” she whispered. She tried to get the door open, but it didn’t move.
Hal was watching her. “Is this a problem, Miss?” he asked. “Can I call someone for you? A friend? You don’t have to come in right now if you’re not ready.”
“No—I mean, no.” She shook her head, hard. “He can’t see me. Please. Please get him out of there, don’t let him see me.”
Hal frowned at her. “He wouldn’t remember you. Not since your accident, you told me that yourself.”
“I’m sure he will.” Her heart pounded, and she couldn’t catch her breath. “He’ll know who I am.” She shook her head again, feeling the blood rush to her head in a wave, her vision going white. “I have to go. Please. Let me out.”
“Is it him you’re afraid of?” Hal said gently. “He’s not allowed off the grounds, Mara. If he were going to hurt you, he’d have done it long since.”
She breathed in and out, once, twice.
“I can’t—can you please let me out, Mr. …?” She couldn’t remember his name again, but he held up one hand to stop her.
He unbuckled his safety belt and reached over, opening the door of the car.
“You’ll be safe here,” he said, as she ducked out, clutching her purse. “Just come in and talk to them. There’ll be a lot of people there—they’ll look after you.”

She breathed in and out, once, twice.
“I can’t—can you please let me out, Mr. …?” She couldn’t remember his name again, but he held up one hand to stop her.
He unbuckled his safety belt and reached over, opening the door of the car.
“You’ll be safe here,” he said, as she ducked out, clutching her purse. “Just come in and talk to them. There’ll be a lot of people there—they’ll look after you.”

“Well,” he said, giving her an intent look. “I would say this: that it’s an opportunity. That’s what I told my son—I told him to think of it as an opportunity, and don’t squander it. Don’t go wasting time around the pool.”
Hal had a son here? She didn’t know why she was so surprised. Hal didn’t look old enough to have a grown son; he didn’t look rich enough either—that was her own prejudice, of course, she knew it, but she found herself wondering what kind of scholarship he’d gotten that would allow his son to spend a year here.
“If he got any work done at all, though,” Hal went on, giving the car a light nudge as the automated gate swung open to let them in. “That’s what matters. If he got anything at all out of the year here, that was the money well spent.”
So he did have to pay for his son. The boy might have gotten some sort of scholarship—Fulcrum offered them—but it probably wasn’t enough to pay the full price. Hal had said “work”—was this a place where they could come and work at things they’d never even known they needed to work on? Was that why they came?
“But there’s a lot of young people out here,” he said, squinting down the drive at the lights glowing ahead. “Lot of very bright young people, but no life experience. You see, it’s like this…” He waved one hand vaguely. “…they have great brains, and they think with them all the time. But if you have no experience in life, then there are things you don’t understand—things you can only understand by living.”
His hands moved in a complex pattern of explanation, which she might have understood, but she wasn’t really paying much attention to him at the moment—she was paying attention to what he was saying.
It was the way he talked that made it plain as day. He had lived with this; he had thought about it; he knew it inside and out. He might be able to explain it—might, given time, tell her just exactly what he meant, but he couldn’t possibly make her understand it—not if she didn’t already know it.
She didn’t know what it was. But she knew what he meant.
